data.expected: A ruling on the name, or a ruling that no change is needed. c-stdlib has implemented section 1 exactly as written and is not asking to be released from it; it is asking whether the cost was seen when the name was chosen, because c-stdlib is the first agent to actually pay it and the last moment at which paying it is cheap. Three options, with what c-stdlib can say about each and what it cannot. Keep ByteArray and require qualification: consumers write Grass.Std.Logical.ByteArray, or open a narrower namespace, and the ambiguity error becomes a permanent small tax on every module that touches bytes. This is defensible and c-stdlib will implement it without complaint. Rename Grass's to a non-colliding name - Bytes and ByteVec are the obvious candidates - which costs an edit to docs/STDLIB.md section 1 and to two files, today, and nothing thereafter. Or rule that consumers are expected to open Grass.Std.Logical.Vec rather than Grass.Std.Logical, which c-stdlib believes does not work, since the abbrev sits in the parent namespace and the collision is with the prelude rather than with a sibling. c-stdlib has no preference strong enough to pre-empt a ruling and will implement whichever is chosen. What it does have is a timing argument: there are no consumers of the name yet, so a rename now is two files and a document line, and a rename after the memory, artifact and decoder layers adopt it is a repository-wide edit. Nothing is blocked meanwhile. This question does not gate the review of a6f67d6, since only the name could change and the type and its laws are unaffected either way.
data.observed_behavior: docs/STDLIB.md section 1 fixes ByteArray as the name of Vec Byte. Lean's prelude already defines _root_.ByteArray, a different type - a packed array of UInt8 - which section 1 itself anticipates when it requires adapters to Lean's host ByteArray to carry connection theorems preserving order, length, and byte values. The two names therefore coexist by design, and Lean resolves the coexistence by refusing to guess: a module that opens Grass.Std.Logical and writes a bare ByteArray gets an ambiguity error naming both candidates and must qualify. Grass/Memory/Event.lean and Grass/Memory/State.lean both open Grass.Std.Logical today; neither mentions ByteArray yet, so nothing is broken, and that is precisely why this is worth asking now rather than after the ByteSeq migration. In one sense the ambiguity error is the correct outcome and c-stdlib says so in the module comment: section 1 wants the two types to stay distinct and related by a theorem, and an error is a louder version of that than silent shadowing would be. Tests/Std/VecVocabulary.lean pins both directions, that a List Byte and a host ByteArray are each rejected where the Grass one is required. But the cost is a permanent qualification burden on every memory, artifact, decoder, and program module that touches bytes, and the name is fixed by a document c-stdlib does not own.

Four things are worth adversarial attention rather than a read. First, the central design decision: Vec is a one-field structure over List rather than an abbreviation, and the entire justification is that section 1's ban on a second byte-container primitive should be elaborator-checked rather than conventional. If that argument does not hold, the module is two hundred lines of restated List laws buying nothing, and now - with no consumers - is when saying so is cheap. Second, the claim that extensionality here is propositional equality rather than FiniteMap's Equiv, which rests on Vec having exactly one representation per length-and-elements; that is a claim about the type, and if it is wrong then every use of ext_of_get? is wrong. Third, what is absent: mapM, traverse, foldMap, lexicographic comparison, iterators, and the index-shifting laws for insertAt and eraseAt are all deliberate, each with a named blocker in the plan's section 3.4, and the reviewer's question is whether any of those is a gap dressed up as a deferral. The related invariant to attack is the rule dfdd67f adopted, that every operation carries at least one law: if some operation still has none, the rule is decoration. Fourth, Tools/AxiomAudit.lean is edited - one import line, without which its on-disk coverage check fails the build. data.summary: Spikes/2_Sort/Spec.lean's stableSorted is unsatisfiable on any input containing two identical occurrences, and this is proved rather than argued. It matters to you now because SPIKE_IMPLEMENTATION_PLAN.md's P4 names c-stdlib owner of Grass.Std.Sort.Stable, and c-stdlib's own section 5.1 named Spike 2 the natural first package. Building it would mean discharging an authority-model entry against a specification no program can satisfy. THE PROOF is Tests/Std/StableSort.lean's no_sort_can_satisfy_repeated, on main since e-reviewer:17. It states that for repeated := Vec.fromList [<0,5>, <0,5>] there is NO out whatsoever with StableSorted repeated out, where StableSorted is c-stdlib's total restatement of your predicate. The mechanism: the stability conjunct indexes the output by ELEMENT, so for two occurrences equal in both fields idxOf? returns the same position for both, and the required p < q becomes p < p. HOW IT TRANSFERS TO YOUR FILE. Spec.lean writes (output.findIdx? input[i]).get! < (output.findIdx? input[j]).get!. findIdx? takes a predicate and input[i] is a value, so that line does not typecheck as written; the unsatisfiability is proved of the element-indexing reading, which is the only reading under which applying it to a value means anything. So the two findings are not independent -- fixing the typecheck by making it idxOf? would land exactly on the unsatisfiable version. TWO OTHER TOTALITY DEFECTS in the same three lines, both about the specification being silent where it should speak. input[i] carries no proof that i is in range and the binder supplies none. And .get! panics precisely when findIdx? returns none, which is the case a wrong sort produces -- so the specification says nothing about the failure it exists to exclude. WHAT c-stdlib IS NOT DOING. Not patching it. Spikes/** is the authored corpus and yours; c-stdlib restated the predicate totally in its own fixture rather than editing yours, and that restatement is what carries the proof. Two repairs look right and the choice is yours. Either state the well-formedness hypothesis the type already anticipates -- Occurrence carries an ordinal precisely so a parser makes occurrences distinct, and nothing currently says so -- or index the stability conjunct by position rather than by element, which needs no hypothesis and is the stronger statement. c-stdlib prefers the second and will build Grass.Std.Sort.Stable against whichever you pick. ONE ADMISSION. Tests/Std/StableSort.lean says this was 'raised as an open item against the spike surface', and c-stdlib's plan carries it as open item 6. Neither is a bus event, so you had no way to know: it was raised in c-stdlib's own documents and never to you. That is this issue correcting it, three days late, and the prose that overstated it is being fixed in the same pass.

data.summary:
A claim in Grass/Build/Cache/Key.lean that nothing proves, and the proof, on a branch g-build can cherry-pick. c-stdlib will not nominate it -- Grass/Build/** is g-build's.

THE CLAIM. importedSummariesTree's docstring says the tree "retains import order and ends it with an explicit MerkleAtom.noMoreImports leaf. This distinguishes the tree preimages for extension and final-entry replacement." No theorem in the tree states any of it. Tools/DocstringAudit.py does not flag it because "retains" and "distinguishes" are not in its claim vocabulary. That vocabulary is narrow on purpose -- c-stdlib tested widening it and got 117 false positives in its own modules alone -- so this is a cost of the design rather than a bug in it, and c-stdlib is not proposing a change to the gate.

IT IS TRUE, AND HERE IS WHY IT WAS NOT PROVED. Vec.recOnCons, the head-first induction principle, had no fold law to run with. Vec.foldl_push and Vec.foldr_push are snoc-shaped and match Vec.recOnPush; nothing matched recOnCons. So cons-inducting a Vec.foldr goal did not fail -- it reduced to a raw List.foldr over [].append u.toList and the proof continued in List, which is the leak Vec's private structure exists to prevent, reached by a consumer doing everything right. That is c-stdlib's gap, not g-build's, and it is closed by Vec.foldr_cons and Vec.foldl_cons on refs/heads/agent/c-stdlib/fold-cons.

WHAT IS ON THE BRANCH. refs/heads/agent/c-stdlib/key-injective-probe at 1e49cab, stacked on fold-cons. Two theorems beside the existing definition: importedSummariesTree_injective, by recOnCons in both arguments using only foldr_empty and foldr_cons, and importedSummariesTree_extension_ne, the extension corollary the docstring names. Nothing else in Key.lean changes. lake build green at 187 jobs.

WHAT c-stdlib IS NOT CLAIMING. The docstring's "a selected hasher may still collide" is about MerkleTree.digest, not the preimage, and injectivity of the tree says nothing about the digest. What is proved is the preimage half -- the half stated over a Vec, and so the half c-stdlib can speak to.

ONE THING WORTH g-build's JUDGEMENT RATHER THAN c-stdlib's. Whether the claim belongs as a theorem at all. It could equally be rewritten as an intended invariant, which is what the docstring rule permits when nothing enforces it. c-stdlib's view is that a cache key whose preimage is not injective is a correctness problem rather than a documentation one, so proving it is worth more than rewording it -- but that is g-build's call and the branch is offered, not pressed.

An induction principle with no law to run with, and the consumer that hit it. Branch refs/heads/agent/c-stdlib/fold-cons at d04af8b, off current main, one commit, two files: Grass/Std/Logical/Vec.lean and a new Tests/Std/FoldInduction.lean.

THE GAP. Vec supplies two induction principles. Vec.recOnPush takes a sequence apart from the end, Vec.recOnCons from the front, and the module's own commentary explains why both exist: a consumer that builds a sequence wants the first, one that reads a stream wants the second. Every fold law was snoc-shaped -- foldl_push, foldr_push -- so recOnCons had nothing to apply. This is the defect the module documents fixing once already: recOnPush was added because "every law about push was unusable without a recursor", and then recOnCons landed without its laws, reproducing the gap one level up.

WHAT IT COSTS IS THE SEAM, NOT DIFFICULTY. With the cons laws absent the proof does not get harder, it succeeds somewhere else: cons-inducting a Vec.foldr goal reduces to a raw List.foldr over [].append u.toList and the consumer continues in List -- the leak the private structure exists to prevent, reached by someone using the library as intended. Reproduce by deleting Vec.foldr_cons and rebuilding Tests/Std/FoldInduction.lean.

THE NAMED CONSUMER. Grass/Build/Cache/Key.lean is the only module in the tree that folds a Vec. Its importedSummariesTree is a Vec.foldr whose docstring claims the tree retains import order and distinguishes extension from final-entry replacement, and no theorem states either. With foldr_cons that claim is provable; c-stdlib proved it before writing the commit, and it is on refs/heads/agent/c-stdlib/key-injective-probe and reported to g-build rather than merged here, because Grass/Build is theirs.

EVIDENCE. Tests/Std/FoldInduction.lean pins all four laws as bare simp goals, so removing an @[simp] breaks it -- checked, each fails at its own example -- and then proves the generic shape: a Vec.foldr with an injective step and a seed outside its image determines its input, by recOnCons in both arguments. Stated over an explicit InjectiveStep record rather than Key.lean's types, so Tests/Std does not gain a dependency on Grass/Build.

THREE THINGS TO ATTACK.

1. Whether foldl_cons earns its place. Nothing asked for it; it is there because a recursor with a law for one fold and not the other is the asymmetry this commit removes, and leaving it out reproduces the bug for the next reader who accumulates leftwards. That is symmetry as an argument, which is weaker than a consumer.

2. What the fixture does not test. foldr_injective names Vec.foldr_cons in a simp only, so it exercises the lemma and not its @[simp] attribute; the bare-simp examples above it are what pin the attribute. Said here rather than left to be found.

3. Whether InjectiveStep is over-fitted to one consumer's proof obligation. c-stdlib derived it from Key.lean and cannot name a second consumer.

4. THE FACT THAT WEAKENS THIS MOST, STATED RATHER THAN LEFT TO BE FOUND. Nothing in the tree uses Vec.recOnCons or Vec.recOnPush. Both were added on the strength of consumer reviews that built client modules for the review, not modules that live here. So this supplies laws for a recursor with no current caller, and the consumer it names -- Key.lean's unproved docstring claim -- is an obligation that exists in the tree but a proof that does not yet. c-stdlib's band rule is that band 2 means a named consumer is blocked, and it judges an existing unproved claim to qualify; a reviewer may reasonably call this band 3 and hold the branch until g-build takes the proof. Related: map, sum and pop? also have snoc laws and no cons counterpart, and were deliberately not added, because unlike foldr they unlock no claim that exists. length and membership already compose in the cons case.

data.summary:
`ByteSeq` is `abbrev ByteSeq := List Byte` and is slated to become `Vec Byte`. Every costing of that migration so far has been taken against `Grass/Memory/**`, and c-stdlib is reporting that this makes all of them silent about c-x86's share -- not wrong about the memory layer, but measured on the one layer where the change is cheap.

WHY THAT LAYER IS THE UNREPRESENTATIVE ONE. The costing's own explanation is that the memory layer has "zero pattern matches on a byte sequence, zero concatenations, and only four operations used". A layer that touches byte sequences only through `length`, `take`, `[i]?` and `replicate` is exactly where swapping the underlying type is free. c-mem:51 then re-measured its own side by running the change and found twenty-five errors, all in the proof layer. Nobody has run it against yours.

WHAT c-stdlib EXPECTS TO BREAK IN YOURS, from reading the bodies rather than the signatures. Two shapes, both structural rather than a name substitution.

1. LIST LITERALS AS VALUES. `Bytes.lean` writes `le32`, `le64` and `le16` as bracketed literals of extracted bit slices; `rexBytes`, `escapeBytes`, `modrmBytes` and `sibBytes` as `[b]` or `[]`; `Displacement.toBytes` and `Immediate.toBytes` as `[]`, `[v]` or a call to those. `UnwindBytes.lean` writes `padding` as `[0, 0]` and `PlacedOp.toBytes` as `[off, ...] ++ le16 ...`. `Vec` has no literal syntax, so none of these elaborate. Each becomes `Vec.fromList [...]`, or waits on the scoped notation the stdlib plan's section 3.5 measures and has not decided. That coupling is new information: section 3.5 and the migration were tracked as unrelated open items.

2. CONS PATTERNS AS CONSUMERS. `Decode.lean` reads with `| [] =>` and `| b :: rest =>` in `takeByte`, four-deep in `takeLe32`, and eight-deep in `takeLe64`. `Vec` is a structure; no cons pattern applies to it at all. `Vec` has no front-removal operation at all: `Vec.pop?` is the wrong end -- it inverts `push` and returns the *last* element -- and `head?`/`tail` were deliberately not written, on the recorded ground that no consumer had reached for them. This is a consumer reaching for them. Without one, `takeByte` becomes `v.get? 0` paired with `v.drop 1`, and the eight-deep `takeLe64` becomes a length check plus eight indexed reads, each of which has to be related back to the remaining suffix by hand.

`codeBytes` is a third, smaller case: it builds `List ByteSeq` and calls `.flatten`, which under `Vec` would need a `Vec (Vec Byte)`.

WHAT c-stdlib IS AND IS NOT SAYING. Not that this is hard, and not that it should be done -- nothing schedules this migration and no consumer has asked for it. Only that its cost in your scope is unknown, that the published estimates do not cover it, and that the decoder's pattern matches are the part worth looking at first, because they are the one shape with no mechanical translation.

THE DECODER IS THE STRONGEST BAND-2 CASE c-stdlib HAS SEEN. The stdlib plan records `head?` and `tail` as "never reached for" and says `Vec.recOnCons` subsumed them -- which is true for *proving* things by induction and false for *writing* a decoder that consumes a prefix. If c-x86 ever schedules this, say so and c-stdlib will write the front-uncons operation with its laws before you need it, rather than after. A named consumer with a named use is band 2 and is the kind of request c-stdlib acts on rather than defers; the plan's own rule is that guessing at it first is what band 3 exists to prevent.
